deep.reconstruction:
The page has no mathematical derivations, formulas or computations. It continues a series of programmatic aphorisms on the nature and role of mathematics, separated by horizontal rules. In order:

(1) The page opens by finishing a sentence from the previous page: mathematics now takes over the role 'which philosophy formerly played'. Only as a mathematician is Hilbert able to deal with both Husserl (philosophy) and Nernst (physical chemistry) at a professional level so that he understands them.

(2) Unity of mathematics. Doing, for example, hydrodynamics may at the same time bring one closer to the prime number problem. Applying the laws of purely logical thought may perhaps also yield the reason for the law of spectral series (Balmer–Rydberg). The awareness of this is called the most sublime [word uncertain] of mathematics.

(3) Methodology. Hilbert opposes superfluous generalisation that repeats old ideas in a less simple and clear form without adding new ones. All good ideas should be demonstrated, worked through and presented in the simplest and most familiar case. He gives a travel metaphor: first learn where you are at home; when you travel, you want to see something new, not merely the old under more complicated conditions.

(4) No Ignorabimus. 'That there is no Ignorabimus in mathematics is probably provable by my theory of logic-arithmetic.' This is a programmatic claim. The solvability of every mathematical problem (the axiom of solvability, Paris 1900) is to be established metamathematically through his joint foundation of logic and arithmetic (cf. Heidelberg 1904). In modern terms this anticipates completeness/decidability questions.

(5) Mathematics walks on earth and touches heaven. The examples are the Müngsten bridge (a steel railway arch bridge opened 1897), the orbits of electrons, and the questions of logic and epistemology.

(6) Theory and experience. They are closely linked subjectively. But the finished theory must be developable objectively without any empirical input, apart perhaps from the minimal 'empiricism' required to build up logic.

Dating, inferred by me: Müngsten bridge (1897), Husserl in Göttingen (from 1901), Nernst in Göttingen (until 1905), electron theory, and 'Menge aller Mengen' on the next page all point to about 1901–1905.
errors: No mathematical errors; the page has no derivations.

The claim that the absence of an Ignorabimus is provable via his logic-arithmetic theory is, in modern hindsight, false in its natural reading. Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) and the undecidability results of Church and Turing (1936) show that no consistent, effectively axiomatized system of arithmetic decides every arithmetical statement. Hilbert hedges with 'wahrscheinlich' (probably).

deep.surprise_reason: These are programmatic notes known in content from Hilbert's published addresses. Mildly notable is the early, explicit link (around 1901–05) between 'no Ignorabimus' and a metamathematical proof through his 'Theorie der Logik-Arithmetik'. This shows the germ of the proof-theoretic solvability aim well before the 1920s, though historians (Peckhaus, Sieg, Corry) know these notebooks.
